papers.title: Enhanced local synchronization with impaired large-scale recruitment of NREM slow waves in pediatric disorders of arousal
papers.abstract: NREM slow waves emerge from the synchronization of neuronal activity across multiple spatial scales. During childhood, local synchronization and large-scale propagation undergo distinct maturational trajectories, paralleling cortical synaptic remodeling and the maturation of long-range brain connectivity. How alterations in this local-to-global organization relate to arousal instability remains poorly understood. Here, we used 256-channel high-density EEG to characterize NREM oscillatory organization in 17 children with disorders of arousal (DOA) and 17 age- and sex-matched healthy controls. Children with DOA showed a marked dissociation between local synchronization and large-scale coordination: slow waves were locally larger, steeper and more synchronized, yet recruited the cortex less globally and exhibited a more spatially restricted distribution of origins. This phenotype preferentially involved Type 1 slow waves, a subtype associated with widespread cortical and subcortico-cortical recruitment and late developmental maturation. Children with DOA also showed reduced centro-posterior slow spindle density, providing convergent evidence for altered coordination of distributed NREM oscillations. These microstructural abnormalities occurred despite largely preserved conventional sleep architecture. Together, our findings reveal an altered local-to-global organization of NREM sleep in pediatric DOA and suggest that vulnerability to incomplete arousals may emerge when strong local synchronization is not matched by effective large-scale network coordination during brain development.

papers.title: The cry as a vital sign: A smartphone based study protocol of neonatal cry acoustics in hypoxic ischemic encephalopathy
papers.abstract: Background. Many Indian special newborn care units (SNCUs) cannot offer amplitude-integrated EEG (aEEG) or early MRI, so bedside judgement decides which newborns receive closer neurological attention. Earlier work found that asphyxiated newborns cry with a higher pitch and shorter phonation than healthy newborns, and a meta-analysis reported higher fundamental frequency, dysphonation and atypical melody in infants with neurological dysfunction, with wide differences between studies. Aim. To determine whether basic acoustic features of a smartphone-recorded pain cry (following a heel prick) can differentiate term newborns with HIE from control newborns. Also, to track changes in cry acoustics over the first 72 hours of life and evaluate their association with the clinical severity and short-term outcomes of encephalopathy. Design. A prospective, single centre diagnostic accuracy and cohort study in a tertiary SNCU. Three groups of term newborns are recorded: newborns with HIE, healthy comparators, and sick comparators who do not have HIE. Every newborn is recorded after the same stimulus, the first clinically indicated heel-prick. Newborns with HIE and sick comparators are recorded again at 24 hours, 72 hours and before discharge. A cry that is late or absent counts as a result and not as a missing value. Three clinicians blinded to group also classify the cries by listening, so the phone-based measures can be compared with the human ear. Analysis. The primary outcome is the area under the ROC curve of a logistic model with five pre-specified acoustic predictors. The target is 180 analyzable newborns (70 with HIE and 110 comparators). Reporting follows STARD and TRIPOD+AI. Relevance. In a South Asian trial, cooling did not reduce death or disability at 18 months and increased death alone. A cry tool in this setting is therefore proposed to help prioritize EEG, seizure surveillance, closer observation and referral. It is not proposed as a trigger for cooling. Keywords: neonatal encephalopathy; infant cry; acoustic analysis; smartphone; diagnostic accuracy; low-resource setting.

papers.title: Part 1 of a 2-part, open-label clinical trial evaluating repeated nicotinamide riboside parenteral administration: 3 consecutive days of intramuscular and subcutaneous injections
papers.abstract: Nicotinamide riboside (NR), an endogenous precursor to the essential coenzyme nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+), is characterized as safe and effective for longitudinally elevating NAD+ in blood and tissues, when administered orally. Interest in alternative routes of administration of NR has increased in recent years and led to the development of pharmaceutical-grade NR for intravenous and injectable administration. To evaluate the safety and efficacy of repeat daily injections of NR, an open-label, pilot, trial was initiated. Utilizing a 2x2 parallel study design, 39 study participants were randomized to intramuscular (IM) or subcutaneous (SC) injection administration, and 50 or 100 mg of NR, for 3 consecutive days, followed by a 7-day washout (50 mg IM, n=7; 100 mg IM, n=11; 50 mg SC, n=11; and 100 mg SC, n=10). To assess the primary outcome of safety, vitals, blood biomarkers, and adverse event monitoring were employed. Additional assessments included NAD+ pharmacokinetics and subjective participant-reported outcomes. Daily injections of NR were well tolerated and did not result in any unexpected adverse events or experiences. Pain and muscle soreness/tightness more than two minutes after the injection were reported by 44% and 41% of the participants, respectively, regardless of the route of administration or dose. Significant heterogeneity of pharmacokinetic parameters for NAD+ augmentation of whole blood was observed, however an average of the daily percentage increases in NAD+ was consistent across treatment groups, resulting in 9.51, 9.97, 7.83, and 9.05% for 50 mg IM, 100 mg IM, 50 mg SC, and 100 mg SC, respectively. Exploratory participant-reported outcomes suggest potential benefits on fatigue and sleep, with mixed effects on global physical health. Repeat daily injections of NR were well tolerated, and findings warrant investigation in larger, powered, placebo-controlled trials.

papers.title: Whole person health across sociodemographic groups of adults in the United States
papers.abstract: Chronic disease accounts for most health care expenditures in the United States (US), highlighting the need for approaches that address health across interconnected spiritual, mental/emotional, behavioral, physical (including environmental), and social domains. Whole person health (WPH) is increasingly recognized as important for alleviating chronic disease burdens but has not been well-described across various sociodemographic groups of US adults. Using cross-sectional data from the 2025 National Health Interview Survey, we sought to describe the prevalence of WPH and its components among US adults overall and by age, sex, and race along with ethnicity. Participants responded to the nine-item Whole Person Health Index (WPHI), which we used to assess continuous scores (range: 9-45, where higher scores indicated improved health) and ''optimal'' (excellent/very good vs. good/fair/poor) overall and domain-specific WPH. Using survey procedures, we estimated medians (IQR) and prevalence (95% CI) and compared subgroups using multiple comparison correction. Among 23,884 NHIS participants aged 18 years and older (mean age (SE)=48 (0.2) years), representing approximately 261,620,640 US adults, the median WPHI score was 33 (28-37) and slightly over half (57% [56%-58%]) of adults were classified as having ''optimal'' overall WPH. Optimal social/family connections (72% [72%-73%]) were frequently reported; ''optimal'' sleep was infrequently reported (36% [35%-37%]). WPH and its components were generally highest among younger adults. Men and women differed in WPH domains but not in overall WPH. Non-Hispanic (NH) American Indian/Native Alaskan and NH-Black adults generally had lowest prevalence of optimal WPH and its components, which was often higher among Hispanic/Latino adults and highest among NH-Asian and White adults. These results showing variation in WPH in the US may inform future investigations of WPH, related predictors and health outcomes, and health disparities.

papers.title: CBD use characteristics associated with perceived effects and satisfaction among CBD product users in Japan: an exploratory analysis of a cross-sectional web-based survey
papers.abstract: Background. Cannabidiol (CBD) products are sold in many forms for many purposes, but it is largely unknown which characteristics of real-world use relate to how users evaluate their experience. Methods. We analyzed an anonymous web-based survey of 377 CBD product users in Japan. We evaluated perceived-effect (0-5) and satisfaction (0-6) scores using main regression models of use frequency adjusted for age, sex, and body mass index. Separate supplementary models examined estimated daily CBD amount and other-cannabinoid co-use, purposes of use, or specific CBD amount-reporting status. Results. Use frequency was positively associated with perceived effects (B = 0.148, 95% CI 0.091 to 0.205) and satisfaction (B = 0.113, 95% CI 0.049 to 0.177; both p < 0.001). Estimated daily amount showed no clear association with either outcome after adjustment, whereas participants who reported specific milligram information had higher scores on both (B = 0.543, p < 0.001 and B = 0.559, p = 0.002). Amount-reporting status was associated with product form (tincture 48.5% vs 30.8%; smoking or inhalation 58.5% vs 75.7%; both FDR-adjusted p = 0.009), whereas no statistically significant group differences were found for age, sex, body mass index, use frequency, or sleep timing. Purposes of use and sleep-timing indicators showed no clear associations with the outcomes. Conclusions. Subjective evaluation of CBD use was more consistently related to how often CBD was used and whether a specific milligram amount was reported than to how much was reportedly taken, and amount-reporting status was related to product form. Specific CBD amount-reporting status may be a useful complementary dimension for characterizing real-world CBD use.

papers.title: Menstrual symptoms and infertility odds among individuals with co-occurring endometriosis and polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome
papers.abstract: Objective: To study the prevalence of co-occurring endometriosis and polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS), estimate infertility odds, and characterize menstrual symptom profiles associated with this combined phenotype in a population cohort. Design: Prospective digital cohort in the United States (US). Subjects: 90,714 consented participants enrolled between November 2019 and June 2025 who completed relevant surveys; a subset of 25,152 participants with menstrual cycle logs linked to monthly surveys contributed to symptom analyses. Exposure: Participants were classified by self-reported physician diagnosis into four groups: endometriosis alone, PMOS alone, co-occurring endometriosis and PMOS (endometriosis+PMOS), or neither condition (reference group). Main Outcome Measures: (1) Odds of self-reported physician-diagnosed infertility (ever/never, cross-sectional), estimated using multivariable logistic regression adjusted for age, race/ethnicity, and subjective socioeconomic status; (2) number of adverse menstrual symptoms logged per cycle, assessed using negative binomial mixed-effects models adjusted for age, race/ethnicity, and hormonal contraceptive use. Results: Among 90,714 participants, the mean age was 35.1 years (standard deviation: 11.6) and the majority identified as non-Hispanic White (72%). Prevalence estimates were 11% for PMOS alone, 6% for endometriosis alone, and 2% for endometriosis+PMOS. Individuals with endometriosis+PMOS more frequently reported unemployment, low socioeconomic status, active smoking, poorer subjective health, early menarche, current irregular cycles, and a broad range of comorbidities. Infertility odds were highest for endometriosis+PMOS (odds ratio: 12.49 [95% confidence interval: 11.13-13.99]), followed by PMOS alone (6.12 [5.69-6.59]) and endometriosis alone (4.31 [3.93-4.72]), with the combined effect exceeding additive expectations (relative excess risk due to interaction: 3.05 [1.65-4.46]). Individuals with endometriosis+PMOS logged 11% more symptoms per cycle than those with neither condition (incidence rate ratio: 1.11 [1.04-1.19]) and had the highest odds of logging pelvic pain, fatigue, and sleep changes, among other symptoms. Conclusion: In this large US digital cohort, co-occurring endometriosis and PMOS affected 1 in 50 participants and was associated with markedly elevated infertility odds exceeding additive expectations, and a heightened menstrual symptom burden. Several risk factors and health impacts characteristic of each condition appeared amplified in individuals with both conditions, suggesting a subgroup with compounded clinical complexity and greater care needs.

papers.title: Part 2 of a 2-part open-label clinical trial evaluating repeated nicotinamide riboside parenteral administration: 90 days of at-home subcutaneous injections
papers.abstract: Nicotinamide riboside (NR), a precursor to the essential coenzyme nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+), has been extensively studied following oral administration, while the longer-term safety and physiological effects of injectable NR remain less characterized. Following an initial in-clinic phase evaluating repeat intramuscular (IM) and subcutaneous (SC) administration of pharmaceutical-grade NR, participants transitioned to an at-home phase designed to assess the safety, feasibility, and exploratory physiological effects of repeated self-administered SC administration. Participants continued their assigned 50 or 100 mg dose group and self-administered NR subcutaneously 3 times weekly for approximately 90 days. Safety was assessed through adverse event (AE) monitoring, vital signs, and clinical laboratory health measures. Exploratory assessments included markers of mitochondrial bioenergetics, urinary biomarkers of oxidative stress, and participant-reported outcomes related to fatigue, sleep, pain, and quality of life. At-home administration of NR was generally well-tolerated, with no clear dose-dependent safety concerns identified over the study period. Further, participants were able to successfully self-administer repeated SC injections over the study period, demonstrating positive feasibility. Whole-blood NAD+ concentrations remained largely stable over time in both dose groups. MeScreen analysis demonstrated a reduction in GlycoATP at Day 30 and increases in the MitoATP/GlycoATP ratio at Day 30 and Day 90, signifying a preferential shift toward oxidative metabolism. These findings may be indicative of positive metabolic health shifts. Urinary oxidative stress profiling demonstrated heterogeneous temporal responses. Several lipid oxidation markers significantly declined at Day 30 but returned toward baseline at Day 90. Select markers of nucleic acid, nitrative stress, and advanced glycation end-product oxidation demonstrated more sustained reductions. These results for which the majority of measured oxidative stress markers improved suggest that NR injections may exhibit anti-oxidative characteristics. Validated participant-reported sleep and fatigue measures showed improvements. Self-reported facial skin improvement increased descriptively from 11.4% at baseline to 27.8% at Day 30 and 36.8% at Day 90; improvements noticed by others increased from 9.1% to 23.7%, while reported body-skin improvement increased more modestly, from 8.8% to 16.7%. As these outcomes were not designed or powered to establish efficacy or definitive clinical claims, the findings should be considered hypothesis generating and provide preliminary data to inform the selection of outcomes and design considerations for future randomized, placebo-controlled, adequately powered trials of SC NR administration.
